clinicalPearls: An indolent marginal-zone B-cell lymphoma that arises primarily within lymph nodes without the splenic or extranodal (MALT) presentation of the other marginal zone lymphomas
Typically presents in older adults with localised or generalised peripheral lymphadenopathy and is often asymptomatic
Diagnosis is one of exclusion, requiring careful demonstration that a splenic or extranodal primary is absent
The neoplastic cells are CD20-positive marginal-zone or monocytoid B cells negative for CD5, CD10, CD23 and cyclin D1
An association with autoimmune disease and, in some cases, hepatitis C virus infection is recognised
The cells may show plasmacytic differentiation, and a small monoclonal paraprotein can be present
Asymptomatic patients may be observed, with anti-CD20 targeted therapy or chemoimmunotherapy and local radiotherapy used for symptomatic or advanced disease
reference.pathophysiology: Nodal marginal zone lymphoma originates from a post-germinal-centre marginal-zone/memory B cell that proliferates within the lymph node, expanding the marginal and interfollicular zones and sometimes colonising reactive follicles. Chronic antigenic and immune stimulation, including autoimmune conditions and hepatitis C virus infection in a proportion of cases, is thought to promote clonal outgrowth. The tumour cells display heterogeneous marginal-zone, monocytoid and plasmacytic morphology and may harbour recurrent mutations affecting NF-kappaB signalling and marginal-zone differentiation. By definition the disease lacks the defining splenic or extranodal features of the other marginal zone lymphomas, although secondary spread to bone marrow or blood can occur.
additionalDifferentials: Splenic marginal zone lymphoma with nodal spread
Extranodal (MALT) marginal zone lymphoma with nodal involvement
Reactive follicular hyperplasia with monocytoid B-cell reaction
additionalInvestigations: Excisional lymph node biopsy for architecture and immunophenotyping
Immunohistochemistry and flow cytometry showing CD20-positive, CD5/CD10/CD23/cyclin D1-negative B cells
Staging imaging to confirm absence of a splenic or extranodal primary
Hepatitis C virus serology and autoimmune screen where relevant
Serum protein electrophoresis for an associated paraprotein
redFlags: Rapidly enlarging node, B symptoms or rising lactate dehydrogenase suggesting transformation to aggressive lymphoma
New extranodal or marrow involvement with cytopenias
reference.prognosis: The disease usually follows an indolent course with prolonged survival, though it is generally considered to have a somewhat less favourable outcome than extranodal MALT lymphoma; the principal adverse event is transformation to aggressive large B-cell lymphoma.
pitfalls: Diagnosing nodal marginal zone lymphoma without excluding a splenic or extranodal primary
Mistaking the tumour for follicular lymphoma when reactive follicles are colonised
Missing plasmacytic differentiation and an associated paraprotein
Overlooking associated hepatitis C virus infection or autoimmune disease
Failing to recognise transformation in a patient with abrupt clinical change
references: British Society for Haematology guidance on marginal zone lymphomas
